entries.commitment: Rejoin the Paris Agreement on the first day of the presidency
entries.context: In a December 12, 2020 president-elect statement, Biden said the United States would rejoin the Paris Agreement on his first day in office. On January 20, 2021, he signed the instrument of acceptance; the Department of State confirmed that the United States officially became a party again on February 19, 2021. This documents the formal reentry, not achievement of emissions targets or broader climate outcomes. Subsequent change: the UNFCCC records a new U.S. withdrawal notification on January 27, 2025, effective January 27, 2026; the United States is no longer a party as of this review. The commitment was originally documented in a president-elect statement after the November 2020 election, not established here as the earliest campaign-trail statement.
entries.action_date_description: United States officially became a party again; acceptance instrument signed January 20, 2021

entries.commitment: Make interest on loans for domestically manufactured automobiles tax-deductible
entries.context: At an October 22, 2024 campaign rally, Trump proposed deductibility of auto-loan interest for qualifying U.S.-built cars. Public Law 119-21 later introduced a deduction of up to $10,000 per year for eligible interest on loans for new, U.S.-assembled personal vehicles, generally for tax years 2025–2028 and subject to eligibility and income limits. Used vehicles and leases do not qualify. This record does not imply that every auto loan qualifies.

At an October 22, 2024 campaign rally, Trump advocated no tax on overtime. Public Law 119-21 later established a temporary federal income-tax deduction for qualifying overtime premium compensation (tax years 2025–2028), with annual limits of $12,500 ($25,000 for joint filers) and income-based phaseouts. The deduction does not eliminate all taxes on all overtime earnings. The record notes a related policy action without treating the campaign slogan as fully enacted.

At an October 22, 2024 campaign rally, Trump advocated no tax on tips. Public Law 119-21 subsequently established a temporary federal income-tax deduction for qualifying tips (tax years 2025–2028), subject to eligibility conditions and a $25,000 annual limit. This is not an exemption from all taxes on tip income; applicable payroll taxes remain. The record documents a related enacted policy, not a determination of full fulfillment or voter intent.
